title: Maryland’s new media advertising law raises serious policy concerns
summary: Strengthening local news is a commendable goal, but the Local News for Maryland Communities Act of 2026 is the wrong way to get there, writes J.H. Snider, who says it is protectionist, pro-incumbent legislation that will corrupt, not cure, independent media.
content:
by J.H. Snider, Maryland Matters May 8, 2026

by J.H. Snider, Maryland Matters May 8, 2026

Media scholars often assert that the decline in local news media will incentivize government corruption. I agree, but it is sad that Maryland’s newly passed legislation to fix that problem will aggravate it.

Passed on the last day of the legislature’s 2026 session, the legislation directs Maryland state agencies to spend 50% of their advertising dollars on local media. The stated goal behind this legislation is commendable: Strengthening Maryland’s local news media. But this protectionist, pro-incumbent legislation corrupts independent media. Sometimes a cure is worse than the disease.

Local news media in Maryland and much of the rest of the United States already receive massive public subsidies and incumbent protections. Notable ones, none of which were mentioned in the legislature’s deliberations, include:

Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.

We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials or political candidates.

Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.

Views of writers are their own.

In both 2025 and 2026, the local news media lobby used The Banner as its star public advocate. This was smart politics because The Banner is a highly regarded nonprofit news outlet that competes with The Baltimore Sun, owned by a conservative publisher unpopular with more than two-thirds of the Legislature. This owner also controls 185 local TV stations across America, including FOX45 in Maryland.

But The Banner is unrepresentative of subsidy recipients. In 2025, it had only 60,000 subscribers out of Maryland’s population of 6 million. The subsidies will primarily go to commercial media, especially local broadcasters, which have larger audiences and are correspondingly more appealing to government advertisers.

Maryland media failed to cover this legislation before it passed. But government organizations provided public testimony that the legislation would reduce their efficiency and effectiveness.

Maryland’s Lottery stated it could reduce its revenue due to lower efficiency in spending its $20 million annual advertising budget. Maryland’s Association of County Health Officers observed that its target population for health information, especially Maryland’s underprivileged, would be harder to reach or unreachable, partly because they don’t subscribe to local media. Maryland’s Department of Transportation warned its safe-driving messages would similarly suffer.

The media lobby asserted that the legislation was revenue-neutral. But protectionist, anti-competitive policies, like Trump’s tariffs, are inflationary.

No media subsidy advocate made an effective case that the subsidy would be spent on local watchdog journalism, rather than serving as a cash cow or being used for other projects such as sports, weather, national news, entertainment programming, acquisitions or paying down debt.

The standard practice when the legislature provides a subsidy to private entities is to establish accountability mechanisms to ensure the subsidy is spent as intended. That wasn’t done here.

Maryland’s media lobby argues that Maryland is copying similar government advertising set-aside policies in New York City, Chicago and San Francisco. But those policies are new and untested; they also have material differences, including eligibility criteria, transparency, geographic scope and effective percentage of mandated media dollars. The media recipients have also inexplicably changed under new mayors.

Illustrative of the risk of media corruption, authoritarian governments, including Turkey, Hungary and Serbia, use government ad subsidies to control media coverage of themselves. This is effective because the media must think twice before biting the hand that feeds them.

Maryland’s local media have long avoided holding their commercial advertising customers accountable. Now we can expect the same for their government advertisers.

The legislature’s stated media policy goals are worthy. But the test of public policies is not their goals; it’s their implementation. Reducing government corruption could be better achieved by other means, such as with a well-designed system of independent inspectors general or by incentivizing Maryland state’s attorneys to go after the powerful rather than only the weak. These approaches would indirectly subsidize democratic accountability journalism, as local news media could use the resulting exposés as a foundation for providing a better news product.

The best solution should be narrowly tailored to the problem at hand. The legislature’s government ad set-aside legislation fails to meet that test.
